cells.tense: You are standing here with the next real move in your hands, and you can see why it works.
cells.act: pick the one you would be sorriest to lose
cells.ask: Name the goal on this road that matters most, the one whose loss would sting longest. Say it plainly to yourself. Then take a step toward it today.
cells.core:
You can see what's under things. Not in a spooky way — you notice the shape a situation is making, and that shape tells you what to do next without the noise. Here, on a road you're holding, the lever is visible to you.

What keeps this honest is choosing a light on purpose instead of drifting toward whatever is loudest. That doesn't need a justification or a proof that the heading is right. Name the goal whose loss would sting longest, and put a foot toward it before the day ends. Doing that once sharpens your reading of the road instead of letting it turn into a story you keep rehearsing about how it might go.

cells.tense: You will have worked out every turn of this road before you have taken the first step.
cells.act: set one rule that makes the rest easier
cells.ask: Set a rule for this direction — a day you stop for the week, an hour it gets, a line past which you won't keep planning. Keep the rule this week.
cells.core:
The pattern-finding has turned on itself. Every branch of the direction gets thought through before a foot moves, and the thinking keeps going because thought doesn't stop by itself. Underneath is a wish for the road to be settled before you commit anything to it.

More insight won't close this. A single rule will. A day you stop for the week, an hour the work gets, a line past which you don't keep planning. That isn't a cage. It's a bank that lets the water go somewhere. Once the thinking has an edge, you can act on the part you can already see, and it stops needing to generate more.

cells.tense: The direction was chosen and you are still standing at the edge of it.
cells.act: join the practice the others keep
cells.ask: Join one standing practice with other people in it — a class, a group, a weekly thing — and show up a few times before you decide whether it's yours.
cells.core:
There's a road you set out on, and you have not got your weight behind it. When you look at it, what shows up is the literal layer: the tasks, the steps, the thing you said you'd do. None of it carries a reason bigger than itself, so nothing pulls you forward.

Effort won't fix that. Contact will. Go to one meeting, one class, one standing thing with other people in it, before you've made up your mind about whether it belongs to you. Find someone who walked this before and ask how they really did it, the unpolished account and not the summary. Direction tends to come back through other people, not through pushing. You don't have to feel it first.

cells.tense: You are the one steering this direction, and you talk about it as if it were running loose.
cells.act: feel it alongside them and keep your own side
cells.ask: Next time someone tells you what they're carrying, feel it with them for a few minutes and keep your own footing. No sorting, no pointing at what you notice. Stay, and stay yourself.
cells.core:
You are steering a whole direction, and the story you tell has it steering itself. The patterns you spot so easily in the work — you don't spot the one where your hand is on the wheel, and nobody nearby has a reason to bring it up.

What's underneath all of it is simple feeling with other people, and that part has gone quiet. The way in is smaller than the direction: sit with one person in what they're carrying, and fix nothing. Not long. The point isn't to help. It's to be reached by them. When you can feel with someone without tidying them, the wheel comes back under your own hands, and you get to know it's there.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the person is steering a direction they can already feel going well — the record only gives the capacity, not that it's aimed anywhere. A reader could reasonably say the direction is someone else's, or that they're only watching, not steering. The asks survive being wrong because each one is a small move you can make even if the reading is off. The sentence that serves me is 'you can build in the dark' — it's an image I like, not anything the record says.
